rationale: Two reference forms that are easy to miss because they are not `$(VAR)`. `$(VAR:.c=.o)` is a `substitution_reference` — a SIBLING of `variable_reference`, not a child — so an analyzer reading only the latter loses every substitution reference in the corpus (9 of them). `$@` / `$<` / `$^` are `automatic_variable`s: they name something no file can declare, which is exactly what the `uses` class exists for, so they are published rather than dropped and labelled `automatic` rather than `builtin`. `$$` is Make's ESCAPED dollar, so `$$?` is the SHELL's exit-status variable, not a Make automatic one; the edge is real information but calling it a builtin would be a category error, so it is labelled `shell_variable`.

forbidRelationships.note: SRC is declared in this file, so the substitution reference to it is a `references` edge; `uses` would demote a real declaration
an automatic variable names nothing any file can declare, so it is `uses`; `references` would claim a declaration named `$@`
an automatic variable is a READ, not a call

a computed name is not DECLARED, so no `contains` edge may claim this file declares it. The declaration belongs to the two concrete names the expansion can resolve to (FLAVOUR_a / FLAVOUR_b), and inventing a symbol for the computed text would assert a referent that does not exist.

the label must be `uses`, not `references`: `references` is emitted iff THIS file declares the name, and no file can declare a name built at expand time. Getting this wrong would publish a declaration that does not exist.

only the `word` HALF of the concatenation. The whole point of the read is that the name is assembled from `FLAVOUR_` AND `$(FLAV)`; publishing the prefix alone records a name that appears nowhere in the file.
